title: Validate Binary Search Tree
prompt:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST).

A valid BST is defined as follows: the left subtree of a node contains only nodes with values strictly less than the node's value; the right subtree contains only nodes with values strictly greater than the node's value; and both the left and right subtrees must also be valid BSTs.

The tree is given as a level-order array where `null` marks a missing child (the standard LeetCode serialization). Your function receives this array directly; the starter code includes a helper that builds the tree from it, so you only need to implement the validation.

examples.explanation: 1 < 2 < 3, so every node satisfies the BST property.

The node 4 is in 5's right subtree, but 4's own right child is 3, which is less than 4 and also less than the ancestor bound of 5 — specifically, 3 must be greater than 4 to be valid there, which it isn't.

constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4]
hints: It's not enough to just compare a node with its immediate children — every node in a left subtree must be less than ALL of its ancestors up to the point where it became a left child, not just its direct parent.

Carry a valid (low, high) range down through the recursion. The root's range is unbounded; when recursing left, tighten the upper bound to the current node's value; when recursing right, tighten the lower bound.
A node is valid only if low < node.val < high. Return false immediately if this fails; otherwise recurse into both children with updated bounds.

solution.approach: Recursively validate each node against a running (low, high) bound inherited from its ancestors. The root has no bound. When moving into a left child, the upper bound tightens to the parent's value; when moving into a right child, the lower bound tightens to the parent's value. A node is valid only if it strictly falls within its inherited bound; the whole tree is valid only if every node passes this check.
